claims.statement: Modern sport, as defined by Guttmann's seven characteristics (secularism, equality of opportunity, specialization, rationalization, bureaucratic organization, quantification, and the quest for records), is discontinuous with ancient Greek and Roman athletic and spectacular practices.
claims.contested_by: Continuity arguments that treat the modern Olympics or modern arenas as direct heirs of Olympia or the Colosseum.
claims.response: Guttmann's framework treats the seven characteristics as emergent with modernity; Young separately demonstrates that the Greek amateur ideal is a modern construction, not an ancient inheritance.

claims.statement: The achievement of modern Western sport is not the arena form itself but the transformation of contest into a rule-bound, quantified, record-seeking activity in which death is not the object.

support.locator: quantification; quest for records; rationalization (2004 ed.)

claims.contested_by: Bread and circuses claims that modern mass sport is essentially continuous with Roman arena spectacle.
claims.response: Architectural and spectacular lineage can be acknowledged; the institutional transformation (published rules, records, death-not-the-object) is the discontinuity that carries the claim.

claims.statement: The Football Association's Laws of the Game (1863) are a published code of thirteen binding rules governing a competitive physical contest, including dimensions of the ground, method of scoring, offside, and prohibitions on carrying, hacking, and handling.

support.locator: Laws 1–13 (complete code as published); definitions of terms
support.note: Primary text verified on Wikisource 2026-08-25. Adoption date (8 Dec 1863) and MCC modelling are secondary historical claims; do not load them on this Tier 1 locator.

claims.statement: The IAAF publishes official world-record progression lists. The 2015 edition, edited by Richard Hymans and Imre Matrahazi, is the eighth edition of that book and tabulates successive marks by event.

claims.statement: Seneca, in a letter warning Lucilius off crowds, says he happened into a midday spectacle (meridianum spectaculum) expecting relief from human blood and found instead "mera homicidia": men with no armor, the outcome of the fighters is death, the crowd crying "Occide, verbera, ure," and, when the show paused, "interim iugulentur homines, ne nihil agatur."

support.locator: heading VII; [1] (vitandum … turbam); [3]–[5] (meridianum spectaculum; mera homicidia; nihil habent quo tegantur / non galea, non scuto; exitus pugnantium mors est; Occide, verbera, ure; interim iugulentur homines, ne nihil agatur)
support.note: Latin Library opened 2026-08-26; same letter on Perseus at Sen.+Ep.+7.3 (continues through 4–5). Seneca is moralizing against the crowd, not a neutral report, and not a typology of executions, venationes, and gladiatorial combat. The letter does not license the phrase "slave death matches." English access copy only: Wikisource Moral letters to Lucilius/Letter 7 §§3–5 (Gummere), not the authority. Do not cite LacusCurtius (Ep. 7 is not hosted there). Kyle and Fagan remain further reading; they do not load-bear. Status remains pending.

claims.statement: Martial's Liber de Spectaculis (conventional title), written for the Colosseum's inaugural games under Titus (80 CE), is a contemporaneous literary source for the building and its opening spectacles.

support.locator: Epigram I (amphitheatre as wonder: all labor yields to Caesar's amphitheatre); cf. Epigram II (site on Nero's lake / Flavian amphitheatre)
support.note: Latin Library text confirmed 2026-08-25. Epigram XXIX (Priscus and Verus) usable for governing-rule argument only with open concession that the volume also celebrates lethal spectacles.

claims.statement: Modern sport published a standard of equal conditions of competition and has repeatedly been held to that standard by internal and external pressure; historical exclusions (e.g., by race, sex, or class) were contested and often overturned by appeal to the institution's own stated rules rather than by rejection of the institution.
claims.contested_by: Claims that modern sport's history of exclusion proves the equal-conditions rule was never genuine.
claims.response: The existence of a published standard that critics and reformers could invoke is itself part of the institutional achievement; exclusions were real and the standard was used against them.
